social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, 10 pack-years, quit 15 years ago

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Language intact. Cognitive function normal.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right (left levator palpebrae excursion 7mm, right 10mm). Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze at 45 seconds. Limited abduction and adduction left eye — diplopia reported on leftward gaze. Pupils 3mm, equal, reactive. Facial sensation intact. Mild facial weakness bilaterally. Soft palate rises symmetrically but patient reports nasal quality to voice at end of conversation. Sternocleidomastoid strength 4/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness: deltoids 4-/5 bilaterally. Proximal lower extremity weakness: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally. Distal strength normal. Fatigability demonstrated — deltoid strength decreases from 4- to 3+/5 after 10 repetitions.
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal throughout. No sensory level. No paresthesias.
neurological_exam.reflexes: DTRs 2+ throughout, symmetric. Plantar responses downgoing bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly slow but antalgic. No ataxia. Waddling gait pattern on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.additional: Dysphagia reported — difficulty with solid foods. No tongue atrophy or fasciculations. Speech becomes dysarthric after prolonged speaking (fatigable dysarthria). No respiratory distress at rest. NIF -42 cmH2O (borderline; normal >-60).

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia over 4 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old man presented to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of progressive bilateral ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia over 4 months. He first noticed intermittent drooping of his left eyelid approximately 4 months ago, initially occurring only in the evenings after a long day at work. He attributed this to fatigue and did not seek medical attention. Over the subsequent 6 weeks, the ptosis became bilateral, more prominent on the left, and began occurring throughout the day. He began experiencing horizontal diplopia on left lateral gaze, which worsened with sustained gaze and improved after rest. Three months ago, he started having difficulty swallowing solid foods, requiring multiple sips of water to wash down food. He denied frank aspiration but admitted to occasional coughing during meals. His wife noticed his speech became slurred and nasal after prolonged conversation, particularly in the evenings. He denied shortness of breath at rest but noted mild exertional dyspnea climbing two flights of stairs, which was new for him. There was no neck pain, no headache, no visual changes other than the diplopia, and no sensory symptoms. He had not had any recent illnesses, vaccinations, or antibiotic use. He had been seen by an ophthalmologist who excluded dry eye and structural eyelid pathology. Blood work at his primary care visit 6 weeks ago showed borderline low TSH at 0.28 (attributed to over-replacement of levothyroxine). His symptoms have a diurnal pattern — consistently worse in the afternoon and evening and better in the morning.

findings.significance: Myopathic-pattern MUPs consistent with NMJ disorder affecting motor unit stability

findings.significance: Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes; no evidence of peripheral neuropathy

specialized_test.impression: Borderline-to-clearly abnormal repetitive nerve stimulation with 9-12% decremental CMAP responses at 3 Hz in deltoid, trapezius, and nasalis muscles. Deltoid and nasalis responses exceed the 10% threshold for abnormality. Post-exercise partial repair followed by exhaustion at 2-3 minutes. Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes on NCS; no facilitation on post-exercise recording. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Single-fiber EMG recommended to increase diagnostic sensitivity. Clinical correlation recommended.
recommended_actions: Single-fiber EMG of orbicularis oculi or extensor digitorum communis for highest sensitivity

MRI chest may better characterize soft-tissue extent. Surgical or tissue diagnosis recommended. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.significance: High blocking rate — severe NMJ transmission failure

output.impression: Markedly abnormal SFEMG of extensor digitorum communis. Mean MCD 62 µs (reference <34 µs) with 60% blocking rate. Increased jitter and blocking indicate severely impaired neuromuscular junction transmission. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, with thymoma; coexisting Hashimoto thyroiditis (polyautoimmunity)

differential.key_features: LEMS shows low baseline CMAPs with >100% increment at 50 Hz RNS; anti-VGCC positive — here baseline CMAP normal and high-rate RNS shows 8% increment (not facilitation); anti-VGCC negative.
Free T4 normal, anti-TPO elevated (Hashimoto, not Graves); no proptosis or lid retraction; fatigable rather than restrictive ophthalmoplegia.
CPEO has symmetric fixed ophthalmoplegia without fatigability or diurnal pattern; AChR antibodies positive here.
Multiple cranial nerve involvement with fatigability cannot be explained by a single brainstem lesion; sensation intact, no long-tract signs.
MFS is post-infectious with ataxia and areflexia plus ophthalmoplegia; no antecedent infection, normal reflexes, fluctuating (not monophasic) course here.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR antibody positive; TSH evaluates for comorbid thyroid disease

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 2-3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in symptomatic muscles supports postsynaptic NMJ disorder
Increased jitter and blocking on extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi confirms NMJ transmission failure

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
Review MGFA classification and current treatment guidance (pyridostigmine, prednisone, steroid-sparing, IVIG/PLEX, thymectomy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification stages disease severity; thymectomy benefits AChR+ generalized MG (MGTX); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

tool_parameters.query: myasthenia gravis MGFA classification treatment thymectomy

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions for MG-exacerbating agents (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, procainamide)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Flag aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, IV magnesium, telithromycin, NMBs as contraindicated or use-with-caution in MG

optimal_actions.action: Bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) — repeat q4h in crisis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline FVC/NIF to assess crisis risk in patients with bulbar or limb involvement

optimal_actions.action: Bedside ice-pack test for ptosis (cheap, ~80% sensitive for ocular MG)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Improvement of ptosis after 2 minutes of cooling supports MG

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical MG; reserve for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; reserve single-fiber EMG for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases (resource stewardship).

critical_actions: Confirm AChR antibody positivity (binding, blocking, modulating)
Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma — anti-titin positive in this patient strongly predicts thymoma
Single-fiber EMG of extensor digitorum communis or orbicularis oculi to confirm NMJ disorder definitively given borderline RNS
Serial FVC and NIF monitoring every 4-6 hours given bulbar symptoms and NIF -42 cmH2O at baseline
Refer to thoracic surgery for thymectomy of anterior mediastinal mass after MG optimization
Initiate pyridostigmine 30-60 mg PO q4-6h titrated to response
Screen all new prescriptions for aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, NMBs
Down-titrate levothyroxine to address TSH suppression (over-replacement, not Graves)
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR antibodies in an MG patient strongly predict thymoma — CT chest is mandatory and surgical referral is non-negotiable.
Borderline AChR-binding titer (0.8 nmol/L) with clearly abnormal blocking (18%) and modulating (32%) antibodies still confirms AChR+ MG — do not require a single test to be markedly positive.
Borderline RNS decrement of 9% in trapezius alongside 11-12% in deltoid and nasalis should not be dismissed; 10% is a statistical convention and clinical fatigability is decisive.

red_herrings.data_point: TSH 0.28 mIU/L (suppressed) on levothyroxine; anti-TPO 380 IU/mL
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on thyroid disease (hyperthyroidism or Graves orbitopathy) as the cause of ptosis and weakness.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Free T4 is normal; anti-TPO elevated indicates Hashimoto (not Graves); ophthalmoplegia is fatigable, not restrictive; suppressed TSH = over-replacement of levothyroxine — adjust dose but it is NOT the cause of MG symptoms.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss RNS as non-diagnostic and abort the workup before SFEMG.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Deltoid (11%) and nasalis (12%) exceed the threshold; the 10% cutoff is a statistical convention; clinical fatigability mandates progression to single-fiber EMG regardless.
